notes:
I've written notes for all 19 verses, but some sources are missing. I didn't open any Lutheran, Orthodox, Pentecostal-specific, Bible Odyssey or NET Bible study-note pages. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter, so those are left out. The Catholic view comes from the Haydock commentary on biblehub, not from newadvent or catholic.com. Most of the material comes from Enduring Word (Guzik), the older commentaries on biblehub and studylight, and Precept Austin.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** The Hebrew literally says the Spirit of God "fell upon" Azariah, meaning a holy inspiration. Azariah appears only in this chapter. Ellicott says it can't be settled whether Oded is the same prophet as Iddo. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- Benson (repeated word for word in Wesley's notes) says the Spirit came to tell Azariah what to say and to help him say it plainly and boldly. He met Asa as the king came home victorious from the war with the Ethiopians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-1.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch say the Iddo theory "has no tenable foundation." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-2.htm
- Kingcomments (a modern Bible-study commentary on studylight) notes that the name Azariah means "him whom the LORD helps." It reminds Asa that he won because the LORD helped him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-15.html

**v. 2:** Guzik says Judah had just won a big victory and might assume God's favour was guaranteed for good, so God stressed the need to keep *abiding* in Him. He also says God does not hide from a heart that seeks Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
- Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: God does not change. When God seems to change, it is really people's attitude to Him that has changed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
- Ellicott suggests another reading: "the LORD *was* with you (in the battle) *because* you were with Him." He calls the seek/forsake saying a favourite formula of the Chronicler. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- The Pulpit Commentary traces the wording back to Deuteronomy 4:29. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-2.htm
- Matthew Henry calls the verse both a comfort and a caution. God is with them only while they are with Him, and that depends on their continuing in their duty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/15-2.html

**v. 3:** Commentators disagree on which period this describes:
- **The time of the Judges.** This is Wesley's reading: "many times" Israel was largely without God, His law and teaching priests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_chronicles/15.htm
  - Guzik quotes Payne for the same view. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
  - The Gospel Coalition devotional applies it to the last years of the Judges and the first years of the monarchy. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/2-chronicles-14-15-revelation-4-haggai-2-john-3/
- **The northern kingdom under Jeroboam.** Gill reports that the Targum (an ancient Aramaic translation) reads it of Jeroboam's calf-worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-15-commentary
- **A truth for any age.** Keil and Delitzsch lay out the competing views. They note the verse has no verb, so it could refer to past or future. They conclude the prophet deliberately gave no date because the truth holds at all times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-2.htm

On "teaching priest," Guzik says priests did much more than offer sacrifices: they were spread among the tribes to teach God's word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/

**v. 4:** Guzik says the Chronicler used this to remind the returned exiles that God restores people who turn back to Him, even after disobedience has brought them low. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/

**v. 5:** Wesley says people couldn't travel safely, as in the days of Shamgar (Judges 5:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_chronicles/15.htm
- Ellicott links "great vexations" to the "confusion" threatened for apostasy in Deuteronomy 28:20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html

**v. 6:** Ellicott says "nation" here means a tribe or clan. He sees a reference to feuds between tribes, such as Ephraim against Gilead or Benjamin against the rest (Judges 12; 20). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- Wesley says it describes civil wars, with one part of Israel destroying another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_chronicles/15.htm

**v. 7:** Ellicott notes the words echo Jeremiah 31:16 and calls this the point of the whole speech. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- Wesley reads it as "keep going": maintain God's worship and root out idolatry, because that is the only protection from disaster. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_chronicles/15.htm
- Guzik quotes Selman: the speech is unusual because it explains earlier Scripture, in the style of a sermon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/

**v. 8:** Guzik says Asa took bold action rather than becoming passive. He did more than remove what was wrong; he also **restored** what was right. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
- Matthew Henry says reform seemed so hard that Asa lacked the courage to try until God assured him of help. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-2.htm
- **Why "Oded the prophet"?** Ellicott suspects these words are a margin note that slipped into the text, since verse 1 names Azariah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
  - Wesley says Azariah was also called by his father's name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_chronicles/15.htm
- **"Restored the altar."** Ellicott thinks this means it was reconsecrated after being defiled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
  - Clarke suggests it was rededicated or enlarged; he doubts sacrifice had stopped until year 15. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/15-8.html

**v. 9:** Guzik says Asa's courage won over faithful people from the north, and the Chronicler told this to encourage the small returned community. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
- Ellicott compares similar moves south under Rehoboam and Hezekiah. He offers ideas on why Simeon is listed, e.g. some of the tribe had moved north. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- The Pulpit Commentary observes that crowds often follow success more than conviction, which shows how much a godly example matters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/15.htm

**v. 10:** The Spanish edition of the Pulpit Commentary says the Feast of Weeks began around the sixth day of this third month (Sivan). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/tpc/2-chronicles-15.html
- Ellicott thinks the Ethiopian invasion was shortly before, perhaps that spring. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html

**v. 11:** Matthew Henry says the sacrifices gave thanks for past favours and asked for more. He adds that prayer and praise are now our spiritual sacrifices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-2.htm
- Ellicott says the gifts dedicated to the temple were taken from the plunder of Abijah's and Asa's victories. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html

**v. 12:** Wesley says the covenant added no new duty, but it deepened their sense of obligation, guarded them against temptation, and let them strengthen one another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_chronicles/15.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls this the first recorded renewal of the wilderness covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-15.html

**v. 13:** Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary say the penalty is the one set in the Law (Deuteronomy 13; 17:2–6). https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/15-13.htm
- Gill limits it to people who stubbornly refused God and served other gods. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/2-chronicles/15-13.html
- Matthew Henry says it covered the stubborn idolater or atheist. He suggests women were named with Maacah in mind, and that she may have signed the covenant and so been spared. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/15-13.html

**v. 14:** Ellicott says the shouting and trumpet blasts made the oath more solemn. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html

**v. 15:** Wesley says times of covenant renewal should be times of joy: being bound to God is an honour, "and the closer, the better." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_chronicles/15.htm
- Guzik sees this as the fulfilment of the promise in verse 2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
- Matthew Poole says "all Judah" means a great number, since some were surely pretending. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-15.htm

**v. 16:** Ellicott says "mother" means grandmother, and that she kept the queen-mother rank into Asa's reign. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- The Homiletical Commentary notes that many reformers are bold in public but too soft at home; Asa was not. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-15.html
- Gustafson says Asa was the first king recorded destroying idols. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-15-commentary

**v. 17:** This seems to contradict 2 Chronicles 14:3, which says Asa removed the high places. Three explanations:
- Guzik: Asa removed the high places dedicated to idols, but not those dedicated to the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
- Ellicott: chapter 14 records what Asa tried to do, and this verse records that he failed because the people clung to their old shrines. "Israel" here means the southern kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- The Pulpit Commentary calls a reference to the northern kingdom possible but "scarcely tenable." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/15.htm

On "fully devoted," Precept Austin says a blameless heart means the overall direction of a life, not perfection. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-15-commentary

**v. 18:** See the plunder note under verse 11 (Ellicott). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html

**v. 19:** Guzik quotes a writer who says there were skirmishes with Baasha but no open war until this point. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-15/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the text originally said "twentieth," not "thirtieth." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/15.htm
- Ellicott says the date doesn't match the figures in Kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html

## Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 2, "if you forsake Him, He will forsake you":**
- **Methodist/Arminian:** Adam Clarke says the verse leaves no room for the "unconditional perseverance of the saints," a doctrine he strongly attacks. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/15-2.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** Gill reads the verse as being about God's presence and help in trouble; forsaking Him means being left to one's enemies. He doesn't take up the perseverance question here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-2.htm
- **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith):** Smith calls it a truth that is "always true of every man." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/15-2.html
- I found no Reformed or Lutheran reply on this specific verse.

**v. 13, the death penalty:** The Pulpit Commentary (Presbyterian-leaning) says religious tolerance was impossible under Israel's theocracy because idolatry was treason. But church and state are not one under the gospel, so neither may kill dissenters. It adds that the Reformed churches of England and Scotland were slow to see this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-15.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/tpc/2-chronicles-15.html

## Other views

**Catholic (Haydock):**
- **v. 2:** The Pelagians (an ancient group the church judged heretical) argued from this verse that people prepare their own hearts for grace. Haydock replies that the verse speaks of outward help. Even read as inner grace, faithful cooperation can earn an increase of grace.
- **vv. 3–6:** Haydock notes that Protestants read these verses as past, but he reads them as prophecy. Its full fulfilment includes the later ages after the Messiah was killed (compare Hosea 3:4 and Matthew 24). He links verse 4 to Romans 11:26.
- **v. 10:** The third month is when Pentecost falls.
- **v. 17:** The remaining high places honoured the true God only. Asa's heart was "perfect" in outward worship, though he sinned later (ch. 16).

All from https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/2_chronicles/15.htm

**Luther:** Keil and Delitzsch report that Luther, along with Clericus and others, took verses 3–6 as prophecy of the future. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/15-2.htm

**Critical and text questions:**
- Ellicott suggests "Oded the prophet" in verse 8 is a slipped-in margin note. He also says the Chronicler changed the wording he took from 1 Kings 15:16 by adding a "not," in order to put a date on the war. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-15.html
- The Pulpit Commentary raises, without endorsing, the idea that verses 3–6 are a post-exile addition that would fit the divided kingdoms best. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/15.htm
- The NET Bible translates verse 2 as "when you are loyal to him." https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/15-2.htm
